chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Saif ibn 'Amirah from Muhammad ibn Marwan from Fudayl ibn Yasar from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, for Allah, Exalted and Glorious, at the breaking of the fast each night of the month of Ramadan are freed slaves whom He frees from the Fire, except for one who breaks his fast on an intoxicant, and whoever drinks an intoxicant, his prayer is diminished for forty mornings; and if he dies during them, he dies a death of ignorance.

key_terms.عُتَقَاءَ: Freed slaves (referring to those freed from Hellfire)
key_terms.مِيتَةً جَاهِلِيَّةً: Death of ignorance (pre-Islamic state of disbelief)

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual consequence of drinking intoxicants during Ramadan regarding prayer and freedom from Hellfire?
ai.summary: In Shia tradition, this narration from Imam al-Baqir (AS) highlights the specific spiritual merit of nightly Iftar in Ramadan, linking divine emancipation from Hellfire to the purity of the fast. The exclusion of those who consume intoxicants underscores the severity of *khamr* in disrupting worship, with the 'diminished prayer' (*bukhisat salahuhu*) interpreted by scholars as a reduction in reward or acceptance rather than invalidation. The mention of dying in *jahiliyyah* serves as a stark warning that consuming intoxicants reverts the believer to pre-Islamic ignorance, nullifying the spiritual benefits of their faith.
